answer: No. A recorded supervision event or completed reconciliation may evidence an activity, but neither alone establishes adequate supervision, proper ownership records or fulfillment of retained responsibility. That conclusion requires an applicable substantive standard and reliable facts showing that the activity and its results satisfy it throughout the relevant period.

support.quote: This UT Code does not have the force of law.

The Commission may modify or relax the application of a requirement in this UT Code if it considers that, in particular circumstances, strict application of the requirement would operate in an unduly burdensome or unnecessarily restrictive manner.

rival_readings: An allocation-focused reading of paragraph 10 emphasises continuing accountability despite outsourcing; a conduct-focused reading asks whether supervision actually occurred; an adequacy-focused reading examines operational soundness and ownership records. None supplies, by itself, a complete discharge test in the retained text.

A combined assessment may consider allocation, conduct and outcomes together, but its precise sufficiency threshold requires justification. Paragraph 11 separately supports examining whether proper records are actually maintained.

A supervision event or reconciliation can contribute to evidence of compliance. Treating its mere occurrence as conclusive would require an additional sufficiency premise not supplied by the retained provisions.
unresolved: No actual supervision or reconciliation evidence is supplied for an identified entity and period.
The applicable standard of adequacy and the facts satisfying it remain unestablished; insufficient evidence does not itself establish breach.
UT 6.11C concerns outsourced valuation and cannot automatically supply a general tokenisation-supervision standard.
The retained sources do not establish that every operational defect defeats paragraph 10 fulfillment, or that a successful isolated check proves continuing fulfillment.
